claims.text: Aging the titanium–nickel-primary high-entropy alloy at 700°C for 3 hours will induce nanoscale coherent precipitates.
The precipitates will be uniformly distributed within the primary matrix.
The precipitates are likely to be intermetallic phases.
Nanoscale precipitates will obstruct dislocation motion at elevated temperature.
Nanoscale precipitates will delay grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperature.
Obstructing dislocation motion will increase yield strength at 800°C.
Obstructing dislocation motion and delaying grain-boundary sliding will reduce creep rate or extend creep lifetime at 800°C.
The aged alloy will have greater high-temperature yield strength than the same alloy without the aging treatment.
The aged alloy will have greater creep resistance than the same alloy without the aging treatment.
The proposed starting material contains titanium and nickel as primary constituents and at least three additional elements, each at 5–35 at%.
Vacuum induction melting followed by homogenization will produce a single-phase matrix in the proposed, otherwise unspecified composition.
Rapid quenching after aging will preserve the proposed aged microstructure for subsequent testing.
Precipitation strengthening is well established in multiple alloy systems.
The hypothesis is limited to melted and homogenized-cast titanium–nickel-primary high-entropy alloys tested around 800°C in inert atmospheres.

contradictions.description: The starting material is called 'as-cast' while also being homogenized, whereas the baseline and control are described simply as as-cast and without post-solidification heat treatment. It is therefore unclear whether the control is homogenized or truly as-cast, so the intervention and control states are not consistently defined.
